newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Immune Response drug development. [CORRECTED 23:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Immune Response drug development. [CORRECTED 23:05 GMT]

text.p: Immune Response Corp is optimistic about winning U.S. approval over the next few years for two drugs, each of which has a potential market of over a million patients, President Dennis Carlo said.

In an interview, Carlo said he sees a "greater than 50 percent" chance the company will be able to seek an accelerated review of its Remune drug for the HIV virus sometime in 1998, after it releases interim trial data.
He also said he sees a "very, very good" chance of approval of its rheumatoid arthritis drug, if Phase III trials, set to begin later this year, confirmed earlier data.
(Corrects to delete reference to Enbrel in above paragraph. Enbrel is being developed by Immunex Corp., not Immune Response Corp..)
Carlo said the Phase III trial results of the arthritis drug will last about a year.

Immune Response, a development-stage company based in Carlsbad, Calif., has 10 products in its research pipeline. Most work by stimulating the immune system, or controlling an overactive "immune response."

Because of this approach, Carlo said its products could be used in combination with other drugs that attack different mechanisms of a disease. The arthritis drug could enhance other treatments, he said, and "easily be a $1 billion a year drug," even if a competitor beat it to market.

A group of companies are in a race to develop the next-generation drug for rheumatoid arthritis, and Seattle -based Immunex Corp is widely considered to be in the lead with its Enbrel drug. Enbrel works by modulating bodily agents that cause inflammation and Immunex has said it hopes to seek approval in 1998.
Asked about Immunex' advanced position, Carlo said, "There's no reason why people can't take two drugs. With these complex diseases, one drug alone often doesn't do it."
The Immune Response arthritis drug works by controlling malfunctioning immune systems that cause joint swelling.

The company's Remune drug for HIV works by augmenting the body's natural defenses against the virus. Carlo said this mechanism separates it from all the other AIDS drugs on the market, which drive down levels of the virus in the body but do not boost the immune system.
Many patients who have used existing drugs to drive down their viral loads to nondetectable levels continue to have low T cell counts, which leave their immune systems compromised.
Carlo said Immune Response is already gearing up for approval of Remune and has a commercial manufacturing facility up and running.
